title: The Retreate (title and occasion)
short: From Silex Scintillans (1650). A 'retreat' is a going back: the speaker longs to return to the innocence of infancy and to the heaven from which the soul came.
body: 'Retreate' means a withdrawal or going back, and the poem turns the word's usual military sense (falling back) into a spiritual ideal: the speaker wants to 'travell back' to his origin. It appeared in the first part of Vaughan's Silex Scintillans (1650), reissued with a second part in 1655; Martin's Oxford edition prints the 1650 text. The opening exclamation recalls the classical beatus ille tradition ('Happy the man who...'), here applied to a lost time instead of a way of life. Martin suggests Vaughan may have known John Earle's 'Character of a Child' (Micro-cosmographie, 1628), which calls a child the best copy of Adam before the Fall and sees him moving further from God as he grows older.

title: Angell-infancy
short: Infancy as an angelic state: the newborn soul, still close to heaven, shines with unclouded innocence.
body: The coined compound makes the child almost an angel, radiant with a light the adult has lost. The idea draws on Christ's sayings about children (Matthew 18:3, 'except ye ... become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven'; 18:10, on the children's angels who behold God's face). Earle's 'Character of a Child', which Martin proposes as a source, likewise sees the child as nearer to God than the adult. Light imagery ('Shin'd', 'bright-face', 'gilded', 'Bright shootes') runs through the poem.

title: second race
short: The earthly life, seen as a second course (race) after a prior existence of the soul in heaven.
body: 'Race' means a course to be run (Hebrews 12:1, 'let us run with patience the race that is set before us'). Calling it 'second' implies that the soul had a first life before birth, with God, a doctrine of pre-existence found in Platonic tradition and in the Hermetic writings that interested Vaughan and his twin brother Thomas. Critics differ on how literally to take it: some see a real Platonic belief, others a devotional fiction or a way of describing baptismal innocence. 'Appointed' stresses that the earthly course is assigned by God. 'This place' (l. 3) is the world.

title: white, Celestiall thought
short: A pure, heavenly thought; white is the colour of innocence and of the redeemed (Revelation 7:14).
body: 'White' signifies purity, as in the white robes of those washed in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14) and in Isaiah 1:18 ('though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow'). 'Celestiall' means heavenly. Before learning to 'fancy ought' (imagine anything) else, the child's mind held only such unmixed thoughts. 'Fancy' here suggests the image-making faculty that will later lead the soul astray. Vaughan's verse often uses whiteness for innocence,.

title: my first love
short: God, the soul's first love; the phrase echoes Revelation 2:4, 'thou hast left thy first love'.
body: The soul has walked only a short distance from God, its first love, and can still look back and glimpse his face. The phrase echoes Christ's reproach to the church of Ephesus in Revelation 2:4. Measuring spiritual distance in miles makes the soul's descent into life a literal journey, prepared by 'race' and continued in 'travell back' and 'ancient track'. 'His bright-face' (l. 10) identifies the first love as God or Christ.

title: some gilded Cloud, or flowre
short: The child gazes for an hour at a sunlit cloud or a flower, finding in them glimpses of eternity.
body: The child's contemplation of natural beauty is a form of prayer: the 'gazing soul' dwells on a cloud gilded by sunlight or on a flower and sees through it to heaven. Vaughan, like Herbert, has a strong sense of the created world as a book of God. The image of the flower anticipates the Romantic attention to nature that later readers linked with Wordsworth.

title: weaker glories ... shadows of eternity
short: Earthly beauties are 'weaker glories', mere shadows or reflections of the eternal reality behind them.
body: The language is Platonic: visible things are shadows of invisible realities (as in Plato's cave, or the doctrine of recollection in the Phaedo). It is also Pauline: earthly things are 'a shadow of things to come' (Colossians 2:17; cf. Hebrews 10:1). 'Weaker glories' concedes that the cloud and flower are glorious, but only faintly compared with the heaven they reflect. The child sees through them because his soul still remembers its first home.

title: taught my tongue to wound / My Conscience
short: Learning to sin with words injures the conscience; speech is the first sign of the fall from infant innocence.
body: An infant (Latin infans, 'not speaking') has not yet learned to speak, and so cannot sin with the tongue. The epistle of James calls the tongue 'a fire, a world of iniquity' (James 3:6). Vaughan imagines his own speech as a weapon turned inward, wounding his conscience 'with a sinfull sound'. The repeated 'taught' (ll. 5, 15) makes sin something learned, not innate, a view that sits uneasily with the doctrine of original sin and has prompted debate about Vaughan's theology.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), James 3:6

title: black art ... sev'rall sinne
short: Black art: magic or necromancy; the adult has learned the sinister skill of assigning a separate sin to each sense.
body: 'The black art' was necromancy or witchcraft, here used figuratively for the expertise in sin that experience brings. 'Dispence' means distribute or deal out, and 'sev'rall' means separate or distinct: a different sin for each of the five senses. The phrasing makes sin a learned, almost pharmaceutical craft (one 'dispenses' drugs). Vaughan, a physician who also translated Hermetic medical works, knew the vocabulary of both magic and medicine; this reading of his background is a suggestion, not something the poem states.

title: fleshly dresse
short: The body as a garment the soul wears for its earthly life.
body: The image of the body as the soul's clothing is ancient and biblical: Paul speaks of being 'unclothed' and 'clothed upon' with a heavenly body (2 Corinthians 5:1-4). The 'dresse' is temporary and opaque, yet the child feels light from beyond it shooting through. The metaphor anticipates the end of the poem, where 'this dust falls to the urn' and the soul is freed from its garment.

title: Bright shootes of everlastingnesse
short: Shafts of light (or new growths) of eternity felt through the body; Martin traces the phrase to Owen Felltham's Resolves.
body: 'Shootes' are darting rays of light, and also young shoots of a plant; both senses fit a poem of light and growth. Martin points to Owen Felltham's essay 'Of the Soule' in Resolves, where the conscience and the apprehension of eternity prove the soul 'a shoot of everlastingnesse'. Vaughan transforms the borrowed phrase into a felt experience: the child senses eternity physically, 'through all this fleshly dresse'. The line is often regarded as the most memorable in the poem.

title: travell back ... that ancient track
short: The speaker longs to retrace the path by which his soul came into the world.
body: The second half of the poem turns from memory to desire ('O how I long'). The 'ancient track' is the way the soul travelled from heaven into life, and also the old path of the righteous (Jeremiah 6:16, 'ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein'). Travelling backward reverses the usual Christian image of life as a forward pilgrimage. Critics have compared Wordsworth's Ode, where heaven 'lies about us in our infancy' and the soul's light fades as it journeys farther from the east.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Jeremiah 6:16
William Wordsworth, 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood' (1807)

title: glorious traine
short: The radiant company (of angels) or the trailing glory the soul left behind when it entered the world.
body: A 'traine' could be a retinue of attendants or the trailing part of a robe. The soul left behind either the angelic company that attended it, or the robe of glory it wore. Wordsworth's Ode famously speaks of 'trailing clouds of glory' at birth, an image readers have often compared, though no direct borrowing is demonstrated; a 2016 article by Takashi Yoshinaka compares the two poems and proposes Coleridge as a possible point of contact between the poets. The 'plaine' where the train was left is the level ground of the soul's first dwelling.

anchor: That shady City of Palme trees
title: City of Palme trees
short: Jericho, 'the city of palm trees', which Moses saw from Mount Pisgah but could not enter (Deuteronomy 34:1-4): heaven glimpsed from afar.
body: In Deuteronomy 34:1-3 God shows the dying Moses the promised land from Pisgah, including 'the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees'; Moses sees it but is not allowed to enter. Vaughan's 'plaine' (l. 23) picks up 'the plain of the valley'. The 'Inlightned spirit', from its first dwelling, can see the heavenly city as Moses saw Canaan. Palms are also emblems of victory and of the blessed in heaven (Revelation 7:9). 'Shady' suggests cool rest in the desert.

title: drunk, and staggers
short: The soul, having stayed too long in the world, reels like a drunkard and cannot walk straight back to God.
body: 'Stay' means a delay, the soul's lingering in earthly life. The image of reeling and staggering like a drunken man is biblical (Psalm 107:27; Isaiah 24:20, where the earth reels like a drunkard). The 'way' is both the road and Christ, 'the way' (John 14:6). Intoxication with the world's pleasures disables the return journey; the parenthetical '(ah!)' gives the line a note of confession.

title: forward motion ... backward steps
short: Unlike those who prize progress, the speaker wishes to go backward, toward his origin in God.
body: The couplet sets the poem's ideal of return against a culture of 'forward motion' (ambition, worldly advance, perhaps even the new philosophy of progress). Vaughan's preference recalls the Platonic idea that knowledge is recollection of what the soul once knew, and the Christian idea of conversion as turning back. The retreat of the title is therefore an advance in spiritual terms. Wordsworth's Ode reverses the motion again, accepting forward growth and finding compensation in 'the philosophic mind'.

title: this dust falls to the urn
short: At death the body ('dust') goes to its burial urn, and the soul hopes to return to God in the same innocent state in which it came.
body: The body is 'dust' (Genesis 3:19, 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return'); the urn is a burial vessel, a classical image for the grave. The closing lines echo Ecclesiastes 12:7: 'Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.' The final line is short and metrically abrupt ('In that state I came return'), as if the return were sudden. The poem's circular structure enacts the desired return.

anchor: Some men a forward motion love
title: couplets
short: Thirty-two lines of octosyllabic (four-stress) couplets, a light, quick metre used for a meditative lyric.
body: The poem is written in iambic tetrameter couplets, the metre of Milton's 'L'Allegro' and 'Il Penseroso' and of much seventeenth-century meditative verse. The couplets give a plain, aphoristic clarity, especially in the paired antitheses of the close ('forward motion' / 'backward steps'). The movement divides into two halves: twenty lines of remembered innocence, then twelve of longing to return, signalled by 'O how I long'.
